identification.summary: Spandex Tempest is Microsoft's name for the financially motivated cybercrime actor that Proofpoint tracks as TA505 and CrowdStrike as MONTY SPIDER [S1]. Proofpoint describes TA505 as responsible for the largest malicious spam campaigns it had ever observed, distributing Dridex, Locky, Jaff, The Trick and other malware at high volume through the Necurs botnet [S2]. From late 2018 the group shifted from ransomware-first spam toward backdoors and RATs (ServHelper, FlawedGrace, Get2/SDBbot) aimed heavily at financial institutions [S3][S4]. Fox-IT reported in 2020 that the group had moved toward running most of its operation itself, from initial infection through monetization, including a Clop data-leak site [S5].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint's timeline begins with Dridex campaigns in 2014 [S2]; the Proofpoint profile was published in September 2017 [S2].
identification.notes: Microsoft maps Spandex Tempest to MONTY SPIDER and TA505 and labels it 'Financially motivated' [S1]. Microsoft separately tracks Lace Tempest (DEV-0950), which it named as the actor behind the 2023 MOVEit Transfer exploitation linked to the Clop extortion operation [S1][S8]. US government advisories use 'CL0P Ransomware Gang, also known as TA505' [S7], so the industry label TA505 spans activity that Microsoft splits between Spandex Tempest and Lace Tempest. Mandiant tracks related activity as FIN11 and several UNC clusters, which it has treated as overlapping with but not identical to TA505 [S9][S11]. MITRE ATT&CK tracks the group as TA505 (G0092).

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor identified in the sources gathered; Microsoft classifies Spandex Tempest as financially motivated [S1]. 2019 reporting on CyberInt research describes TA505 as believed to be Russian-speaking [S10].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft's mapping assigns TA505 and MONTY SPIDER to Spandex Tempest [S1]. The 'Russian-speaking' characterization is a vendor belief reported in press coverage, not a government attribution [S10].
attribution.basis: Microsoft naming taxonomy [S1]; Proofpoint campaign tracking from 2014 onward [S2][S3][S4][S6][S12]; Fox-IT analysis of Get2/SDBbot samples [S5]; CyberInt research as reported by SecurityWeek [S10].

objectives: Financial gain through banking-trojan fraud, ransomware, remote-access tooling on financial and retail networks, and data-theft extortion [S1][S2][S3][S5]. Proofpoint describes the actor as opportunistic and trend-setting, changing tactics to follow the most profitable targets [S6].

regions: Global, not focused on a single region [S3]
Financial institutions in Greece, Singapore, UAE, Georgia, Sweden and Lithuania (Sept 2019) [S4]
Financial institutions in Chile, India, Italy, Malawi, Pakistan and South Korea, and US retailers (Dec 2018 to Feb 2019) [S10]
targeting.notes: Proofpoint assessed in 2019 that TA505 focused on financial institutions while alternating with wider campaigns against other verticals [S4]. Victim counts in the CISA Clop advisory (3,000+ US and 8,000+ global organizations) are attributed to the 'CL0P Ransomware Gang, also known as TA505' and should not be assigned to Spandex Tempest alone given Microsoft's separate Lace Tempest cluster [S7][S1].

capabilities.summary: High-volume malspam via the Necurs botnet delivering Dridex, Locky, Jaff, GlobeImposter and Philadelphia [S2][S12]. FlawedAmmyy RAT delivered through Quant Loader in 2018 [S12]. Delphi-based ServHelper backdoor and the full-featured FlawedGrace RAT (first observed November 2017), delivered by Word, Publisher and PDF lures in late 2018 [S3]. Get2 downloader from September 2019 delivering FlawedAmmyy, FlawedGrace, Snatch and the C++ SDBbot RAT [S4]. Abuse of the commercial Remote Manipulator System remote-administration tool against banks and retailers [S10]. HTML redirects in the infection chain and a 'CL0P^_- LEAKS' data-leak site by 2020 [S5]. In 2021, intermediate loaders written in Rebol and KiXtart (tracked by Morphisec as MirrorBlast) replaced Get2 and delivered an updated FlawedGrace [S6].

campaigns.name: Locky ransomware via Necurs
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint attributes large Locky campaigns, alongside Dridex, Jaff and The Trick, to TA505 using the Necurs botnet.

campaigns.name: GlobeImposter and Philadelphia ransomware
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint profile reports TA505 elevating GlobeImposter and Philadelphia from regional ransomware to global threats.

campaigns.name: FlawedAmmyy via Quant Loader after Necurs downtime
campaigns.summary: After Necurs disruption in early 2018, Proofpoint reports TA505 resumed Necurs-driven campaigns delivering FlawedAmmyy RAT.

campaigns.name: ServHelper and FlawedGrace introduction
campaigns.summary: Phishing waves in November and December 2018 delivered the ServHelper backdoor and FlawedGrace RAT to banks, retail and restaurants.

campaigns.name: RMS RAT campaign against banks and retailers
campaigns.summary: CyberInt reported Remote Manipulator System use against financial institutions in six countries and US retailers through February 2019.

campaigns.name: Get2 downloader and SDBbot RAT
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint observed Get2 from 9 Sept 2019 and SDBbot from 7 Oct 2019, with Excel lures to financial institutions in several countries.

campaigns.name: Resumed GetandGo/SDBbot campaigns and Clop leak site
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT reported resumed campaigns using HTML redirects and the launch of the CL0P^_- LEAKS site for non-paying victims.

campaigns.name: Accellion FTA exploitation (Clop/FIN11-linked; cluster boundary disputed)
campaigns.summary: Zero-day exploitation of Accellion FTA with DEWMODE web shell, attributed by CISA to the Clop gang 'also known as TA505'; Mandiant tracked it as UNC2546 with FIN11 overlaps.

campaigns.name: Return with MirrorBlast loaders and new FlawedGrace
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint reported renewed high-volume email campaigns using Rebol and KiXtart loaders and an updated FlawedGrace.

campaigns.name: MOVEit Transfer exploitation (Microsoft: Lace Tempest, not Spandex Tempest)
campaigns.summary: CISA attributes CVE-2023-34362 exploitation with LEMURLOOT to the Clop gang aka TA505; Microsoft named Lace Tempest. Listed for context only.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated cybercrime actor tracked as Spandex Tempest / TA505 / MONTY SPIDER, reported as believed Russian-speaking [S1][S10].
diamond.capability: Necurs-delivered malspam; Dridex, Locky, GlobeImposter; FlawedAmmyy, ServHelper, FlawedGrace, Get2, SDBbot; Rebol/KiXtart loaders; commercial RMS tool [S2][S3][S4][S6][S10][S12].
diamond.infrastructure: Necurs botnet for spam distribution [S2][S12]; actor-registered domains with recurring naming patterns [S6]; HTML redirect pages and a Clop data-leak site [S5].
diamond.victim: Banks and financial institutions worldwide, retail, restaurants and hospitality, and broad multi-industry recipients [S3][S4][S6][S10].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven operations that follow the most lucrative monetization model, from banking fraud to ransomware and data-leak extortion [S5][S6].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints opened via Office macro, PDF and MSI lures; payment-heavy retail and banking networks [S3][S6][S10].

gaps: Microsoft has not published, in sources found, a dedicated Spandex Tempest profile; the Microsoft name is supported only by the MSTIC naming mapping [S1].

Cluster boundary: Microsoft separates Spandex Tempest (TA505) from Lace Tempest (DEV-0950, Clop/MOVEit), while CISA treats the CL0P gang as 'also known as TA505' and Mandiant uses FIN11/UNC clusters. Accellion, GoAnywhere and MOVEit activity is not confirmed as Spandex Tempest by Microsoft [S1][S7][S8][S9][S11].
Russian-speaking assessment comes from vendor reporting via press; no government attribution of nationality or state nexus located [S10].

Primary documents could not be opened (fetch blocked or DNS failure): Proofpoint blogs, Fox-IT/NCC Group article, CISA AA23-158A, Canadian Centre for Cyber Security TA505/Cl0p profile; details rely on search-result summaries.
Activity attributable specifically to Spandex Tempest after 2021 is not established in the sources gathered.
Imported actor record lists country RU; this is not confirmed by Microsoft, which labels the group only as financially motivated [S1].

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: The operational environment is email gateways, user Windows endpoints and, for support functions, financial and payment systems such as finance offices, base retail and contractor payroll [S3][S10]. STEP 2: High-volume campaigns of tens to hundreds of thousands of emails can overwhelm filtering, and the actor swaps loaders and payloads often, which shortens the useful life of signatures [S4][S6]. STEP 3: The doctrinal template is an Office, PDF or MSI lure, then a loader (Get2, Rebol/KiXtart), then a RAT (FlawedGrace, SDBbot, ServHelper, FlawedAmmyy, RMS), followed by monetization through fraud, ransomware or Clop-branded data-leak extortion [S3][S4][S5][S6][S10]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic phishing that reaches DoD-adjacent finance or contractor users for credential and remote-access theft. MDCOA is ransomware or data-leak extortion against a mission-support contractor that degrades logistics or payroll during an operation. Candidate indicators: macro-enabled Excel or Word lures themed on invoices or insurance claims; MSI execution spawning Rebol or KiXtart interpreters; unexpected RMS/TektonIT remote-admin binaries; HTML redirect chains in phishing links [S3][S6][S10].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: include commodity-crime loader and RAT families in DODIN threat reporting, because this actor's tooling changes yearly [S4][S6]. (2) Authorities: this is a criminal, financially motivated actor [S1], so response will be primarily DCO-IDM and law-enforcement coordination rather than an adversary-state military response. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize contractors and support functions that handle payment and personnel data, given the actor's banking and retail focus and its data-leak extortion model [S3][S5]. (4) Coordination: track vendor naming differences (Spandex Tempest, TA505, Lace Tempest, FIN11, CL0P) in joint reporting to avoid double-counting or merging separate clusters [S1][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: TA505, the name given by Proofpoint, has been in the cybercrime business for at least four years. This is the group behind the infamous Dridex banking trojan and Locky ransomware, delivered through malicious email campaigns via Necurs botnet. Other malware associated with TA505 include Philadelphia and GlobeImposter ransomware families.
